Saturn orbiter (~2523 kg dry) + Huygens descent probe (~318 kg, ESA-built, landed on Titan 2005-01-14)

© NASA / JPL-Caltech / ESA / ASI / Space Science Institute — joint U.S. / European public-domain mission. Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years (2004-2017), completing 294 orbits and 162 close moon flybys. Highlights: Huygens landed on Titan 2005-01-14 (first soft landing in the outer solar system); discovered Enceladus's plumes 2005 (~100 geysers from the south-polar tiger stripes); resolved Saturn's hexagonal polar storm; mapped Titan's lake system via radar; first observation of seasonal change on Saturn (Cassini covered nearly half a Saturnian year). Grand Finale (2017-04-23 to 2017-09-15) — 22 ring-gap orbits + atmospheric entry that destroyed the spacecraft over Saturn's cloud tops, ending the mission for planetary-protection reasons (preventing future biological contamination of Enceladus or Titan).

Titan IVB / Centaur lifts the 5712 kg Cassini–Huygens stack from Cape Canaveral toward a 6.7-year VVEJGA cruise — too heavy for a direct shot at Saturn, so four planetary gravity assists do the work the chemical engine cannot.

First of four assists (1998-04-26). Cassini sweeps 284 km above Venus, stealing 7 km/s of orbital velocity from the planet to raise its aphelion outward. Total mission ∆v is fixed; this exchange is what makes Saturn reachable.

Second Venus encounter (1999-06-24), 623 km altitude, after a Deep Space Manoeuvre that re-shaped the orbit. The two Venus assists together raise the aphelion past Earth, setting up the third assist 55 days later.

1171 km above the South Pacific (1999-08-18) — the closest planetary flyby of any outbound interplanetary mission to date. The orbit is now energetic enough to cross Jupiter's, where the final assist will deliver Saturn.

9.85 million km from Jupiter on 2000-12-30, simultaneous joint observation with Galileo (in Jovian orbit). Jupiter's gravity bends the trajectory the last 2.5 km/s needed to ride a Hohmann-like transfer to Saturn 3.6 years later.

96-minute main-engine burn (2004-07-01) slows the spacecraft from 30.5 km/s hyperbolic to 23.7 km/s, capturing into a 116-day orbit. The 13-year Saturn tour begins. Huygens will release toward Titan five months later.
13 years in orbit around Saturn — Huygens landed on Titan 2005-01-14 (first outer-solar-system soft landing)

Cassini did what no spacecraft had done at any giant planet: it stopped. For thirteen years it lived at Saturn, and the discoveries that mattered most came from staying — the geysers of Enceladus, caught because the orbiter flew close enough, often enough, to see a tiny moon venting its hidden ocean into space. It dropped Europe’s Huygens probe onto Titan, the only landing ever made in the outer solar system, and charted a world of methane rivers and lakes. At the end, out of fuel, it was flown deliberately into Saturn so it could never fall onto the ocean moons it had found and contaminate them — a mission that closed by protecting the places it discovered.

Joint NASA-ESA-ASI mission. After a 7-year cruise using gravity assists at Venus, Earth, and Jupiter, Cassini entered Saturn orbit 2004-07-01 and operated for 13 years, completing 294 orbits and 162 close moon flybys. It discovered Enceladus’s south-polar plumes (active water-ice geysers), mapped Titan’s methane lakes via radar, and resolved Saturn’s hexagonal polar storm. The Grand Finale (April–September 2017) wove 22 orbits through the gap between the rings and the cloud tops, ending with a controlled atmospheric entry to prevent any chance of contaminating Enceladus or Titan with terrestrial microbes.
Titan IVB / Centaur lifts the combined Cassini-Huygens stack.
